Elon Musk promises a SpaceX share to every child in the US next year

With roughly 72–73 million people under the age of 18 in the US, Musk’s one-time gift would be valued at about $10.5 to $10.7 billion as of now.

Himanshi Aggarwal

19 October, 2026 06:06 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

With roughly 72–73 million people under the age of 18 in the US, Musk’s one-time gift would be valued at about $10.5 to $10.7 billion as of now | X: Elon Musk

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

New Delhi: Elon Musk has promised to distribute a share of SpaceX to each child in the United States of America next year. His announcement on X came hours after AI giant Anthropic detailed plans to dedicate a significant portion of its equity to serve the public.

“Next year, I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America. This will be the first of many,” Musk wrote in a post on X.

SpaceX shares are currently trading at around $146-147. With roughly 72–73 million people under the age of 18 in the US, this one-time gift would be valued at approximately $10.5 to $10.7 billion according to current prices. However, Musk is yet to release details on eligibility, distribution mechanics, tax treatment, or any restrictions on the shares.

Show Full Article

SpaceX was founded by Musk in March 2002, and he currently holds a 48.4 per cent stake in the company, representing roughly 6.42 billion shares valued at over $860 billion to $900 billion.

Also read: France’s unrest reaches the Louvre as protesters block the iconic museum

Following Anthropic’s footsteps Musk’s charity pledge followed Anthropic’s announcement on Sunday, a day before his announcement.

Anthropic, the developer of the Claude AI models, structured as a public benefit corporation, said it would commit 5 per cent of its shares (subject to stockholder approval) to a new Anthropic Public Benefit Fund.

“It will start off with 5 per cent of our shares. For every 50 per cent increase in the company’s value over a set baseline, we can contribute up to an extra 2 per cent, subject to our board’s discretion,” they wrote in a post detailing the scheme. “In total, this means that roughly 20 per cent of Anthropic’s shares are committed to public good.”

The post highlighted that the co-founders have already pledged to donate 80 per cent of their equity, and nearly half the employees are also donating a portion of their equity as part of a donation matching program. The company emphasized that none of the equity held by the fund will be used for lobbying or will be given to political parties.

“I recommend giving the shares directly to the public,” Musk had written in response to Anthropic’s post adding , “This is what I will be doing.”

His follow-up post on Monday specified that children in the US would be the initial recipients of SpaceX equity.

The announcements arrive amid heightened scrutiny of AI companies over safety risks, job displacement, the environmental footprint of large-scale computing, and other concerns.

Despite the charitable pledge, Musk has a history of high-profile pledges that he does not follow through with, Bloomberg noted.

In October 2021, Musk challenged the United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) to provide an open-source spending plan showing how $6 billion of his wealth could solve world hunger. When they gave him a breakdown, Musk did not follow through with his promise.

(Edited by Janaki Pande)

VATICAN CITY, Oct 19 (Reuters) – Pope Leo will hold a general audience with pilgrims at the Vatican on Wednesday for the first time since undergoing surgery for lung cancer, the Vatican said.

The 71-year-old pontiff had an operation on October 13 to remove the lower lobe of his right lung, fuelling speculation about how his illness might change his 17-month papacy.

Leo pledged on Sunday, in his first public event since the surgery, that he would slowly resume his usual activities as the leader of the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics.

Show Full Article

The pope hosts a general audience with pilgrims on most Wednesdays of the year. It is either held in St. Peter’s Square or indoors, depending on the weather.

Twelve migrants, including infant, drown as boats capsize off Greek islands

Reuters

19 October, 2026 03:00 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

Oct 19 (Reuters) – Twelve migrants drowned in two separate incidents off the Greek islands of Lesbos and Samos in the northeastern Aegean Sea on Monday, after their boats capsized as the coast guard chased them, authorities said.

Five men and one woman died after a speedboat carrying migrants from Turkey made a sudden manoeuvre and overturned roughly four nautical miles north of Samos, the Greek coast guard said.

Fourteen men survived and a search-and-rescue operation was under way. Authorities arrested one of the survivors, an Iranian national, on suspicion of migrant smuggling.

Show Full Article

Earlier, four men, one woman and an infant died when their boat collided with a Greek coast guard vessel and overturned off the area of Agrilia in Lesbos. Eight survivors were taken to hospital.

Authorities arrested a 37-year-old Turkish national who was among the eight survivors and identified him as the suspected smuggler and operator of the boat.

The government vowed “zero tolerance” towards migrant smugglers, whom it blamed for the deaths.

On the incident off Lesbos, Greece’s shipping minister Vassilis Kikilias said evidence so far indicated the speedboat struck the left side of a coast guard vessel with its bow, adding that the exact circumstances were under investigation.

“Our position is non-negotiable: zero tolerance for smugglers,” he said in a post on X.

Greece, for years a favoured gateway to Europe for migrants and refugees from the Middle East, Africa and Asia, was at the front line of Europe’s migration crisis in 2015-2016 and nearly 1 million people landed on its islands, mainly from Turkey.

It has since toughened its stance and has been accused by human rights groups of forcibly returning migrants and asylum-seekers on its sea and land borders, a practice it denies, saying its coast guard acts with full respect for human lives and rights.

(Reporting by Renee Maltezou and Antonis Pothitos; Editing by Lincoln Feast and Xevi Fontdegloria)

Trade friction aside, US and Indian firms are building together

US and Indian firms continue to pursue investments, semiconductor partnerships and defence deals despite trade tensions, tariffs and sanctions.

Kriti Upadhyaya

19 October, 2026 10:01 am IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

File photo for representation | Reuters

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

T rade tensions have dominated the US-India relationship over the past year, but the headlines tell only part of the story. American firms continue pursuing production and technology partnerships in India, while Indian companies invest in US manufacturing. Even as Washington and New Delhi struggle to settle trade terms, businesses on both sides continue to bet on each other.

That contrast is evident in IndUS Tech’s review of 14 issues of DOT Weekly covering the third quarter of 2026. Of the 58 developments tracked, industry agreements and licenses formed the largest category with 13 entries. Trade friction has not stopped companies from making long-term industrial commitments and building together.

Building together The tracker recorded 13 industry agreements and licenses, compared with four defense procurement and platform milestones. Only two of the latter were new contracts. India signed a $45.7 million Javelin anti-tank missile purchase and a $204.5 million lease of two MQ-9B SeaGuardian drones. Weeks after the Javelin purchase, Tata Advanced Systems and the Lockheed Martin-Raytheon Javelin Joint Venture signed an MoU to explore production in India.

Show Full Article

HAL reported resolving technical issues surrounding the proposed co-production of 99 GE F414 engines, while Honeywell licensed GMR Aero Technic to maintain components on LEAP engines. In addition, Boeing Defence India partnered with Merlinhawk Aerospace to sustain sensors on Indian platforms, including the P-8I.

India’s procurement policies are shaping these arrangements. The Defence Acquisition Council’s September approvals envisaged sourcing roughly 98 percent of their value from Indian industry. Foreign manufacturers are competing for India’s transport aircraft requirement through Indian partners: Tata with Lockheed Martin’s C-130J and Mahindra with Embraer’s C-390.

Indian firms are also entering international supply chains. MIDHANI became the first Indian company to secure GE Aerospace’s S400 approval for materials testing. Sigma Advanced Systems secured a $104.9 million order from a North American customer for 147,000 extended-range 155mm ammunition shell bodies.

Semiconductors were another area of activity: Microchip Technology signed an agreement involving Kaynes Semicon and GridCrest Technologies on an India-based semiconductor initiative, while Silvaco agreed to provide design tools through C-DAC.

In space, a different collaboration model is emerging. On 2 October, four Indian startups reached orbit aboard SpaceX’s Transporter-18 mission. One of the satellites carries NVIDIA computing hardware that allows customers, including a US-based customer, to run AI models on imagery in orbit. Indian startups are bringing their own technology, payloads, and intellectual property while the US provides launch services, advanced computing, and access to commercial customers, helping these young companies validate their technology in orbit and turn it into viable businesses.

In civil nuclear energy, India issued the draft SHANTI rules which seek to address longstanding supplier-liability concerns that have hindered foreign reactor projects and US-India nuclear cooperation since the signing of the nuclear deal.

Graphic by Shruti Naithani | ThePrint Capital flows Disclosed investment commitments and funding rounds reached $20.45 billion, with capital moving in both directions. The largest came from Essar Group’s US subsidiary, Mesabi Metallics, which announced plans for a $15 billion steel mill in Iowa. In India, Applied Materials announced plans to invest $5 billion over a decade in semiconductor research, suppliers, infrastructure, and workforce development. Marvell committed another $250 million over three years to expand semiconductor R&D and facilities in Bengaluru and Hyderabad.

US investors also targeted Indian defense and aerospace companies. Carlyle agreed to acquire 60 percent of Micropack in a reported $124 million transaction. Norwest co-led Raghu Vamsi Aerospace Group’s $40 million Series B, while Greenoaks led drone maker Airbound’s $37 million Series A. Separately, Skyroot Aerospace was reportedly in advanced talks with US investors to raise capital, although no financing had been completed.

Mesabi Metallics and Applied Materials account for nearly 98 per cent of the disclosed total, and their commitments represent planned rather than completed investment. The smaller funding rounds, however, demonstrate investor interest in Indian aerospace manufacturing and autonomous systems.

The friction The tracker also recorded nine trade measures, and six sanctions and export-control developments. On 13 July, India prohibited imports produced using forced labor. Washington subsequently imposed an additional 10 percent Section 301 tariff on Indian goods under its forced-labor investigation. India credited its engagement with securing a reduction from the proposed 12.5 percent rate and said approximately 45 percent of its exports to the US remained exempt.

India also changed UPI merchant charges, which the US Trade Representative had previously criticized. Indian officials denied that the change was made under US pressure. The rollout of the new merchant fee, initially scheduled for 15 October, was subsequently postponed until after Diwali. Meanwhile, new US drone tariffs excluded India from preferential rates, and three named Indian solar manufacturers and their primary international trading partner Kowa Company Ltd, a Japanese conglomerate, faced a 107.17 per cent cash-deposit rate following US trade investigations, pending a final injury ruling.

On the sanctions front, Washington removed four Indian firms from Russia-related sanctions lists and granted relief relevant to ONGC Videsh’s Venezuelan operations. It also sanctioned an Indian travel company for allegedly supporting Iran’s Mahan Air and later targeted four India-based companies and three Indian nationals over alleged Iran-linked petroleum trade.

The most critical development was a new bill passed with bipartisan support. On September 18, President Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, authorizing tariffs of up to 100 per cent on major buyers of Russian oil and gas, subject to presidential waiver authority. India was not named but remained potentially exposed at the end of the quarter.

Negotiations nevertheless continued, with Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal meeting US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer toward the quarter’s close.

Channels stay open Defense and diplomatic engagement remained active across bilateral and multilateral forums. Of ten military exercises and operations involving both countries, eight were multilateral. This includes two Quad activities – an Indo-Pacific logistics tabletop exercise in Tokyo and a coast guard ship-observer mission between Chennai and Perth.

Bilaterally, Yudh Abhyas spanned two theatres and included the first deployment of the US Army’s M-LIDS counter-drone system to India. At Tarang Shakti, US F-35s exercised with the Indian Air Force from Indian soil for the first time. The period also saw 14 high-level engagements, including two calls between Prime Minister Narendra Modi and US leaders and a bipartisan House delegation visiting New Delhi.

The trade relationship remains unsettled, and not every announced investment or industrial partnership will materialize. But the quarter’s evidence shows companies moving ahead with manufacturing, technology licensing, supplier qualification, and investment. While Washington and New Delhi negotiate the terms of trade, firms on both sides are not waiting for a deal to build together.

Editor’s note: This is a quarterly series tracking key developments in US-India trade, business, technology and defence ties. Read all the articles here.

Kriti Upadhyaya is the manager and founder of IndUS Tech JGJ Ventures LLC, an advisory firm in Washington, DC, and publisher of DOT Weekly. Subscribe to DOT Weekly: https://www.theindustech.com/contact-us. She tweets @upadhyaya_kriti. Views are personal.

(Edited by Prashant Dixit)
